summary: Defines a SASL authentication mechanism that uses SecurID hardware tokens, or software emulations of them, so such tokens can be used in protocols that support SASL. It only authenticates the user and does not protect the data afterward. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Some people carry a small gadget showing a changing number as their key. This explains how programs can accept that changing number as proof of who you are, though it does not hide anything you send.

questions: how to use securid tokens with sasl
how does securid two-factor authentication work
subtitle: Using SecurID tokens for authentication in SASL-enabled protocols

tldr.problem: SecurID hardware tokens are widely used for two-factor authentication, but they could not be used directly with protocols that support SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) authentication.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a SASL mechanism named SECURID that lets clients authenticate by sending a one-time passcode generated by a SecurID token, along with optional user identity and PIN information.
tldr.outcome: The SECURID SASL mechanism provides a standard way to use SecurID tokens for authentication in SASL-enabled protocols like IMAP, ACAP, POP3, and LDAPv3.

today: RFC 2808 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It defines how SecurID tokens can be used with SASL, though this RFC does not mandate implementation in any protocol; adoption depends on individual systems choosing to support the SECURID mechanism.

sections.title: What SecurID and SASL Are
sections.content:
A SecurID token is a hardware device (or software that copies it) made by RSA Security that shows a different number every 30 or 60 seconds. It provides two-factor authentication: the user must have the token and know a PIN to generate a valid passcode. SASL is a framework that protocols use for authentication.

This RFC defines how to use SecurID tokens in any protocol that speaks SASL, such as IMAP (email), ACAP (configuration), POP3 (email retrieval), and LDAPv3 (directory access). The mechanism provides only authentication and does not protect the data that follows, so it must be used with a secure connection if privacy is needed.
sections.eli5: SASL is a way protocols say 'prove who you are.' This RFC lets them ask for a SecurID number as proof.

sections.title: Two-Factor Authentication
sections.content:
The authentication model involves three entities: the user with a SecurID token, an application server that the user wants to access, and an authentication server that checks the credentials. The system uses a shared secret (seed) stored both on the token and on the authentication server, plus a personal identification number (PIN) that the user knows.

To authenticate, the user's token generates a passcode using the seed, the current time, and the PIN. The client then sends this passcode to the server. The authentication server verifies the passcode by checking if it matches what was generated at that time with that seed and PIN.
sections.eli5: Both the token and the server have a secret. You add your PIN to unlock the secret, and it makes a number that only lasts a minute. You send that number to prove you are you.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
The client starts by generating credentials using local information: the seed on the token, the current time, and the user's PIN. If the protocol supports it, the client sends these credentials right away, along with optional identity information. The credential message contains an authorization identity (who this user acts as), an authentication identity (whose token is being used), and the passcode.

The server verifies the passcode and responds with success or failure. If the server needs another passcode (for example, if clocks are out of sync), it requests a new one. If the server needs the user to set a new PIN, it sends a PIN request, optionally with a suggested PIN. The client generates the new credentials and sends them again.
sections.eli5: You send your number to the server. If it says yes, you are in. If it says 'try again,' you make a new number and try once more.

sections.title: Security Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC plainly states that this mechanism only protects against passive eavesdropping (someone listening to network traffic). It does not provide session privacy (keeping subsequent messages secret), server authentication (proving the server is legitimate), or protection from active attacks like man-in-the-middle attacks where an attacker pretends to be the server to capture a passcode.

To protect against such attacks, clients should verify that the server is authentic. When PINs are transmitted, the authentication should happen on a server-authenticated, confidentiality-protected connection. Servers must protect against replay attacks (an attacker replaying a previous valid passcode) and race attacks (an attacker guessing the remainder of a passcode and racing the user to complete the authentication).
sections.eli5: This method only hides from people listening. It cannot stop someone pretending to be the server. Use it only over an encrypted, trusted connection.

sections.title: Passcode and PIN Limits
sections.content:
The specification imposes several constraints on the data. The authorization identity field must be no longer than 255 octets, terminated by a NUL (zero) byte, and must consist of UTF-8-encoded printable characters only. The authentication identity has the same constraints.

The passcode must be at least 4 octets and no longer than 32 octets, terminated by NUL, and must be UTF-8-encoded printable characters (typically 4 to 8 digits). When the server requests a new PIN, the client must respond with both a passcode and the new PIN, each within the same size limits. A suggested PIN from the server, if provided, must also be between 4 and 32 UTF-8 characters.
sections.eli5: The number you send must be short enough to fit in a message and must be readable characters, not random bytes.
